tldr: By modeling hydrodynamic forces, moments, and added mass of a complex underwater vehicle–manipulator system in a differentiable form using spherical harmonics and matrix identification, this work achieves optimal coordination of thruster forces and arm joint torques via gradient-based whole-body model predictive control (MPC).
hero_caption: Pipeline from offline CFD analysis to whole-body MPC. Load data from steady translational/rotational flows and oscillatory CFD are fitted to spherical harmonics and an added-inertia matrix. Closed-form Jacobians are derived and integrated into whole-body MPC using Feasibility-driven Differential Dynamic Programming (FDDP).
overview:
In underwater vehicle–manipulator systems (UVMSs), strong dynamic coupling exists between the floating base and the arm. Conventionally, decoupled control—hovering the vehicle in place while moving only the arm—has been the standard practice. However, whole-body MPC that treats both as a unified system is essential to extend the workspace and distribute actuator loads effectively. Even so, underwater robots often feature complex open-frame geometry. Hydrodynamic forces (drag, lift, added mass, etc.) change drastically with the direction of motion. While computational fluid dynamics (CFD) accurately captures these loads, it is far too computationally heavy to evaluate inside an online MPC loop. At the same time, conventional diagonal damping models cannot capture directional dependencies or cross-coupling.

To solve this, the authors propose a smooth, analytical hydrodynamic model identified from CFD data that yields closed-form derivatives. Spherical harmonics model steady hydrodynamic loads, while an exponential map guarantees energy dissipation (positive resistance). An oscillatory CFD procedure identifies the coupled added-inertia matrix. As a result, analytical Jacobians can be evaluated extremely fast through multibody equations of motion (e.g., using Pinocchio).

Evaluations confirm that the model accurately predicts CFD loads in unseen directions not included in the training data, avoiding the step-size issues and computational burden of numerical differentiation. Furthermore, real-time whole-body MPC paired with an observer to compensate for unmodeled errors and disturbances was tested in the independent marine simulator "Stonefish". The robot completed a 108-second helical tracking task with zero actuator saturation, reaching a high tracking precision of 7.80 mm position RMS error.
contributions: Formulated a differentiable steady hydrodynamic model that captures direction-dependent drag, lift, and moments using smooth spherical harmonics fitted to CFD data, while mathematically guaranteeing positive energy dissipation.
Identified a coupled added-inertia matrix from oscillatory CFD, deriving a formulation that properly separates and synthesizes inertia biases between pure and coupled motions.
Derived complete closed-form analytical Jacobians when combined with floating-base multibody dynamics, enabling integration into an FDDP-based optimal control loop.
Demonstrated closed-loop whole-body MPC in an independent physics simulator (Stonefish), utilizing hydrodynamics for motion allocation rather than merely rejecting them as disturbances.

sections.heading: Why Underwater Robots Need "Differentiable Hydrodynamics"
sections.summary: Highlights the importance of whole-body MPC for coordinating vehicle and manipulator systems, pointing out that no accurate, differentiable hydrodynamic models previously existed for integration into the prediction loop.
sections.details:
An underwater vehicle–manipulator system (UVMS) is a floating-base multibody system where thrusters and joint motors are dynamically coupled. Moving the arm generates reaction forces on the vehicle. Moving the vehicle extends the arm's reach. For compact and lightweight robots where the vehicle and arm have comparable inertia scales, this dynamic coupling cannot be ignored.

Conventional approaches typically rely on "decoupled control," holding the vehicle at a fixed station while operating only the arm. However, this prevents flexible whole-body coordination, such as extending the arm's workspace or using the vehicle's inertia to distribute actuator loads. Applying whole-body MPC—which has achieved remarkable results in legged robotics—allows thruster forces and joint torques to be optimized simultaneously over the same prediction horizon.

The main bottleneck here is the hydrodynamic model. Gradient-based optimal control requires dynamics and their derivatives (sensitivities) at each node across the prediction horizon. Open-frame vehicles experience hydrodynamic forces that vary dramatically with motion direction. High-fidelity CFD captures this well, but its computational cost is far too prohibitive for online optimization loops. Conversely, textbook diagonal damping models fail to capture direction-dependent coupling. This paper bridges that gap by introducing a compact, analytically differentiable hydrodynamic model endowed with the rich expressiveness of CFD for whole-body MPC.

sections.heading: At the Intersection of Whole-Body Control, Hydrodynamic Identification, and Differentiable Multibody Systems
sections.summary: Reviews prior work across three fields—whole-body control of UVMSs, hydrodynamic modeling for optimization, and differentiable multibody algorithms—clarifying how this paper integrates and advances them.
sections.details:
This research stands at the crossroads of three existing research fields.

### II-A Whole-Body Control of UVMSs
Prior UVMS control work has proposed prioritized hierarchical control and MPC with coupling compensation. However, most previous studies treated the vehicle as a base to keep as stationary as possible, seeking to suppress hydrodynamic forces as disturbances. This work sets itself apart by treating the vehicle and arm as equal optimization targets and actively using hydrodynamics in motion allocation.

### II-B Hydrodynamic Models for Optimization
In naval architecture, spherical harmonics have been used to regress surge, sway, and yaw forces. This paper extends that concept to 3D forces and moments in all directions. It provides a formulation that mathematically guarantees positive drag (energy dissipation) essential for optimal control stability, along with closed-form Jacobian derivations.

### II-C Differentiable Multibody Optimal Control
Recursive multibody algorithms like Pinocchio and solvers based on Feasibility-driven Differential Dynamic Programming (FDDP) like Crocoddyl have seen major success in legged robot whole-body MPC. This paper extends that framework to seamlessly embed buoyancy, 3D direction-dependent hydrodynamic loads, and coupled added-mass tensors into multibody sensitivity propagation.

sections.heading: Smooth Hydrodynamic Modeling via Spherical Harmonics and an Added-Inertia Matrix
sections.summary: Steady hydrodynamic loads are smoothly modeled using spherical harmonics and combined with a coupled added-inertia matrix identified from oscillatory CFD, yielding an analytically differentiable model that guarantees positive energy dissipation.
sections.details:
Here is a detailed look at the core hydrodynamic modeling structure.

### III-A & III-B Relative Velocity and CFD Sampling
Let $\mathbf{n}$ be the unit vector representing the relative water velocity direction in the body-fixed frame. In steady CFD simulations, flows are sampled across 32 pairs of directions (64 directions total) on the sphere for translation and rotation. The force vector $\boldsymbol{\lambda}$ is decomposed into an axial force (drag) along the direction of motion and a transverse force (lift) using the projection matrix $\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{I} - \mathbf{n}\mathbf{n}^\top$.

### III-C Modeling Scalar and Vector Fields with Spherical Harmonics
To estimate the drag area $d = C_d A$, 4th-order real spherical harmonics (25 basis functions) are used. A key technique here is linearly fitting the logarithmic drag area $\log d$ and mapping it back with an exponential ($d = \exp(\sum w_j \phi_j)$). This ensures that the drag area remains strictly positive for any motion direction, guaranteeing physically consistent energy dissipation.

Meanwhile, the transverse force coefficient $\mathbf{t}$ is represented as a vector field obtained by projecting the gradient of spherical harmonics onto the tangent plane, keeping it strictly orthogonal to the direction of motion. Rotational moments are modeled analogously, strictly satisfying dissipative properties in pure translation and pure rotation.

### III-D Coupled Added-Inertia Matrix
The added-mass effect from accelerating surrounding fluid is identified via sinusoidal oscillatory CFD, separating velocity-dependent and acceleration-dependent terms via their phase difference. Rather than a conventional diagonal approximation (6 decoupled DOFs), the method identifies a $6\times 6$ symmetric positive-definite matrix $\mathbf{A}_C$ (21 parameters) coupling forces and moments to accurately capture cross-coupling behaviors.

### III-E Closed-Form Jacobian Derivation
Spherical harmonics can be differentiated analytically as polynomials. By applying the chain rule, Jacobians of the hydrodynamic loads with respect to vehicle linear and angular velocities are obtained in complete closed form. They remain smooth near zero velocity and avoid the small-step-size tuning and cancellation errors of numerical differentiation.

captions.F2: Direction-dependent response in the body frame. (a) Translational drag area, (b) rotational resistance, and (c) directional response of the identified added-mass tensor. Larger mesh radii indicate greater hydrodynamic resistance or added inertia in that direction, clearly demonstrating geometric anisotropy.

sections.heading: Multibody Dynamics Integration and Whole-Body Optimal Control Formulation
sections.summary: Embeds the identified hydrodynamic model into the equations of motion for a floating-base multibody system, deriving discrete-time action operators and derivative propagation. Solves for simultaneous thruster and joint optimization using FDDP.
sections.details:
Explains the integration of the hydrodynamic model into whole-body control.

### IV-A Statics and Actuation
Gravity accounts for each link's parameters, while buoyancy is computed from total displaced volume $V$ and a fixed center of buoyancy $\mathbf{r}_{CB}$, transformed to the vehicle base frame. Thruster configuration and joint torques are mapped to generalized forces via the actuation matrix $\mathbf{B}_u$.

### IV-B Discrete Action Model and Derivative Propagation
The rigid-body mass matrix $\mathbf{M}_{RB}$ is combined with the base-frame added-inertia matrix $\mathbf{A}_B$ to construct the composite mass matrix $\mathbf{M} = \mathbf{M}_{RB} + \mathbf{E}^\top \mathbf{A}_B \mathbf{E}$. For the hydrodynamic Coriolis and centrifugal term $\mathbf{b}_A$, a clever bias correction formula subtracts pure translational and rotational components to avoid double-counting with the steady CFD model.

Integrating these dynamics with semi-implicit Euler integration (time step $\Delta t = 30$ ms), the Jacobians $\mathbf{F}_x, \mathbf{F}_u$ of the state transition mapping $\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = \mathbf{f}_d(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k)$ are propagated analytically via recursive algorithms.

### IV-C Shooting Solver and MPC Operation
Feasibility-driven Differential Dynamic Programming (FDDP) is employed for optimization. It searches for solutions along the horizon and warm-starts by shifting previous solutions. To closely match hardware conditions, an augmented state model is also formulated, incorporating thruster dynamics with first-order lag (time constant $\tau_T = 0.18$ s) and rate limits (thrust slew rate $45$ N/s).

sections.heading: Predictive Accuracy, Computational Speed, and Closed-Loop Tracking Performance
sections.summary: Validates hydrodynamic force predictions on held-out CFD directions, compares Jacobian speed and accuracy against numerical differentiation, and demonstrates high-precision closed-loop whole-body MPC in the independent simulator Stonefish.
sections.details:
Multi-faceted evaluations were conducted on a model combining a BlueROV2 Heavy platform and a 4-DOF Reach Alpha 5 arm.

### V-A Load Prediction in Unseen Directions (Cross-Validation)
Cross-validation was performed using 8 directions omitted during identification as test data. The directional error for principal translational forces averaged $4.08^\circ$, with a median moment direction error of $3.79^\circ$, showing high accuracy. Incorporating the coupled added-inertia matrix accurately reproduced load waveforms (amplitude and phase) under oscillation, drastically improving the NRMSE from 97–100% when added mass was neglected.

### V-B Derivative Accuracy and Online Computation Time
Comparing the analytical Jacobians against central finite differences showed exact agreement down to the order of $10^{-9}$. Hydrodynamic kernel derivative computations were substantially faster and more accurate than numerical differentiation, with the full multibody action derivative (including added inertia) taking only $0.165$ ms. This ensures that the full-horizon FDDP optimization loop easily completes within the 30 ms control cycle.

### V-C Vehicle-Arm Coordination and Thrust Allocation
In offline optimization where only an end-effector trajectory (helical motion) was specified, the vehicle handled most of the translational speed ($0.48$ m/s), while orientation adjustments were coordinated between the arm and vehicle (Fig. F5). When water currents were present, riding the current reduced thrust consumption (impulse) by $13.3\%$. Using the direction-dependent model cut thrust by $7.9\%$ compared to an isotropic drag model, automatically generating energy-efficient motions that exploit hydrodynamic characteristics.

### V-D Application in Independent Simulator "Stonefish"
The MPC was evaluated in the Stonefish environment, which uses an independent hydrodynamics engine. A simple load bias observer was introduced to bridge model discrepancies between the simulator and prediction model. Without the observer, end-effector position error was $106.44$ mm, but with the observer, it dropped sharply to $0.49$ mm. In a 108-second (12-revolution) helical tracking task across 3,600 replanning steps, the solver never diverged or saturated thrust, achieving excellent tracking with a position RMS error of $7.80$ mm and an orientation RMS error of $0.98^\circ$.

captions.F5: Results of offline whole-body trajectory optimization accounting for added mass. (a) Six pose snapshots along the 54-second helical trajectory. (b) Translational velocity is led by the vehicle, and (c) yawing motions—such as around 24.8 s where the vehicle and arm counter-rotate to maintain end-effector orientation—demonstrate skillful coordinated movements automatically generated by the optimizer.

sections.heading: Synergy Between Hydrodynamic Prediction and Feedback Control
sections.summary: Discusses the complementary roles of proposed model predictions and real-time feedback, highlighting the advantage of using hydrodynamics for motion allocation rather than treating them only as disturbances.
sections.details:
The key to success in this work lies in the proper division of labor between model prediction and feedback.

Because direction-dependent drag and coupled added mass can be accurately predicted, the optimizer can determine which heading minimizes drag and which accelerations save thrust, distributing natural motion across the vehicle and arm. Meanwhile, unmodeled minor discrepancies arising from real ocean environments or simulators are promptly corrected by high-rate replanning and the load bias observer.

By making hydrodynamics accurately differentiable, this approach moves past conventional control that merely cancels water forces as disturbances, opening the door to whole-body optimal control that actively exploits hydrodynamics as part of the dynamics.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Future Outlook
sections.summary: Summarizes the integration of CFD-based differentiable hydrodynamics with whole-body MPC, highlighting its utility in real-time closed-loop control and potential future directions.
sections.details:
This paper introduced a differentiable hydrodynamic model for underwater robots using spherical harmonics and a coupled added-inertia matrix identified from CFD data. It demonstrated high predictive accuracy for unseen flow directions and fast, exact Jacobian evaluation in complete closed form, successfully integrating with multibody dynamics.

In tasks defined solely by target end-effector trajectories, optimal coordination between the vehicle and arm and thrust savings were achieved, with high-precision tracking confirmed in an independent simulation environment. Future work includes deployment to physical hardware and more detailed modeling of hydrodynamic interference caused by varying arm configurations.

takeaways: Complex direction-dependent hydrodynamics of open-frame underwater robots can be compactly formulated while preserving positive energy dissipation using spherical harmonics (fitted in log space) and a coupled added-inertia matrix.
Closed-form analytical Jacobians eliminate the step-size tuning issues and computational overhead of numerical differentiation, propagating multibody sensitivities in around 0.16 ms.
Incorporating hydrodynamics into dynamics predictions allows whole-body MPC to autonomously choose low-drag headings, reducing thruster effort.
Model discrepancies with the simulator or real environment are robustly compensated for by combining high-rate MPC replanning with a simple load bias observer.
limitations: Hydrodynamic identification primarily targets the vehicle hull; direction-dependent forces on arm links and shadowing effects where arm pose alters flow around the hull remain approximations.

Prior offline identification requires extensive steady and oscillatory CFD runs (64 directions each for translation and rotation, 32 oscillatory axes), requiring significant setup effort for a new robot.
Experimental validation was conducted up to a high-fidelity physics simulator (Stonefish); real-world validation under severe wave and turbulence conditions remains future work.
